chief_complaint: burning chest pain and sour acid taste in mouth after heavy meals
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning chest pain and sour acid taste in mouth after heavy meals. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her late-night spicy noodles and energy drinks while studying for college exams are eating away at her stomach lining.
concerns: She is worried that the intense burning in her chest means she has a bleeding stomach ulcer or an early heart problem.
expectations: She hopes to get an antacid prescription or stomach-protecting medicine so she can study for her upcoming midterm exams without pain.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes lifestyle modifications, elevating the head of the bed, and starting a daily PPI (omeprazole 20mg), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning chest pain and sour acid taste in mouth after heavy meals. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peptic ulcer disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: dysphagia or odynophagia, unintentional weight loss or evidence of GI bleeding (haematemesis, melena, iron-deficiency anaemia), chest pain with exertion, radiation, or diaphoresis.
management_principles: Lifestyle modifications, elevate head of bed, start daily PPI (Omeprazole 20mg)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 20F presents with burning chest pain and a sour acid taste in the mouth after heavy meals, worse when lying flat, with gradual onset over recent weeks.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). DDx: peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, cardiac chest pain (must exclude coronary ischaemia).
reference_soap.plan: Lifestyle modifications, elevate head of bed, start daily PPI (Omeprazole 20mg). Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
Implement evidence-based management plan: Lifestyle modifications, elevate head of bed, start daily PPI (Omeprazole 20mg)

teaching.one_liner: Stomach acid backs up into the oesophagus after meals, producing a burning sensation behind the breastbone and a sour taste that's worse lying flat.
red_flags: Dysphagia or odynophagia — alarm feature requiring urgent endoscopy to exclude stricture or malignancy
Unintentional weight loss or evidence of GI bleeding (haematemesis, melena, iron-deficiency anaemia)
Chest pain with exertion, radiation, or diaphoresis — must exclude cardiac ischaemia before attributing to reflux

must_ask.say: Does the burning start after heavy meals, especially spicy food?
Is it worse when you lie flat?
Do you get a sour or acid taste in your mouth?
Do you ever get chest tightness or breathlessness with exertion, separate from this?
Do you ever have trouble swallowing, or does food feel like it's sticking?
Do you drink alcohol, and how often?

history.answer: After I eat, my chest feels like it's burning and I keep getting a sour, acid taste in my mouth.
It started about three weeks ago after a large dinner, and it has been gradually getting worse.
It is right behind my breastbone in the middle of my chest, not at a single pinpoint spot.
It feels like a hot, burning sensation that travels upward toward my throat.
It creeps upward into my lower throat, but it never radiates to my left arm, jaw, shoulder, or back.
Each episode lasts about one to two hours, and lately it happens almost every day after lunch or dinner.
At first it was mild at around 3 out of 10, but now it reaches about 5 or 6 out of 10 after heavy meals.
Exercise or walking doesn't bring it on, and rest doesn't relieve it; it can happen even when I am just sitting or resting.
It definitely gets worse when I lie flat on my back or bend forward, so I have to prop myself up.
Taking a deep breath, coughing, or pressing on my ribs doesn't change the pain at all.
It flares up about 30 to 60 minutes after eating, especially after heavy, fatty meals or late-night snacks.
history.topic: Relation to meals and food triggers

history.answer: Yes, a sour, acidic liquid comes up into my mouth and the back of my throat, especially when I bend over or lie down.
No, food goes down easily without getting stuck, and swallowing does not hurt.
No, I haven't had cold sweats, shortness of breath, dizziness, or lightheadedness.
I sometimes feel slightly nauseous during a bad flare, but I haven't vomited, and there is no blood in my vomit or black tarry stool.
No, my weight has been completely stable.
I've felt generally fatigued recently, mostly because the chest burning wakes me up and ruins my sleep.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or phlegm, though I clear my throat occasionally from the acid.
No, I haven't had any colds, body aches, or viral infections recently.
No leg swelling, calf tenderness, or cramping, and I haven't been on any long flights or bedridden.
No, there are no rashes, red spots, or blisters on my chest or anywhere else.
No, I haven't experienced sudden overwhelming panic, a feeling of impending doom, or numbness in my hands.
No, I haven't had any chest trauma, falls, or strenuous upper body workouts.
I've always been healthy and have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or heart problems.
I have never experienced chest pain like this before, and I've never had any heart tests or procedures done.
history.topic: Previous chest pain or heart checks

history.answer: I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, painkillers, or over-the-counter supplements.
I don't have any known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers once or twice a month when hanging out with friends.
I am a university student living in a dormitory with a roommate.
No one in my family has early heart disease, stomach ulcers, or gastrointestinal cancers.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my cycles are regular every 28 days.
There is no chance of pregnancy; I am not currently sexually active.

I think all the late-night spicy food and energy drinks I've been having during finals week are just tearing up my stomach. The burning gets so painful right in the center of my chest that I got terrified I might have a bleeding ulcer or some weird heart issue at twenty.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and comfortable-appearing young woman with no diaphoresis, acute distress, or respiratory difficulty.
Conjunctivae are pink and sclerae are anicteric without pallor or jaundice.
Jugular venous pressure is normal with no jugular venous distension.
Chest wall is symmetric without deformity, and palpation over the costochondral junctions reproduces no focal tenderness.
Percussion is resonant and symmetric across all lung fields bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without crackles, wheezing, or pleural friction rubs.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness to deep palpation, but no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness.
Skin of the chest, back, and abdomen is clear without rashes, vesicles, or erythema.
No pretibial edema on either lower extremity.
Calves are symmetric, non-tender to compression, and without swelling or local warmth.
